question:
Patient note:
A 60-year-old man employed as a warehouse inventory supervisor presented to the emergency department at 07:25 after experiencing two abrupt bouts of dark, coffee-ground-appearing emesis that filled roughly half of a two-liter soda bottle he grabbed in panic while walking from the loading dock to his office. He reported that the nausea struck without warning; he leaned forward, retched forcefully, brought up granular material mixed with thin streaks of clotted blood, and then sat on a pallet jack until a co-worker could drive him in. He denied dizziness, tunnel vision, fainting, or falling at any point during or after the vomiting and stated that he remained fully alert enough to lock the building before leaving. The patient said his last bowel movement earlier that morning was medium-brown and formed and looked “normal for me.” Review of recent history revealed moderate alcohol intake in his twenties with subsequent abstinence and a diagnosis of chronic hepatitis C genotype 1b discovered nine years earlier; he completed a full course of ledipasvir-sofosbuvir three years ago, achieved a sustained virologic response, but follow-up ultrasound six months ago still showed nodular contour of the liver and mild splenomegaly consistent with compensated bridging fibrosis. He has never required paracentesis, has no known variceal band placements, and takes no prophylactic non-selective beta-blocker because surveillance endoscopy last year revealed only small caliber, non-bleeding varices. He has stable Stage 2 chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.1 mg/dL), well-controlled essential hypertension managed with amlodipine 5 mg nightly, and mild seasonal allergic rhinitis for which he uses intranasal fluticasone. He has never been diagnosed with congestive heart failure, displays no lower-extremity edema on long shifts, and can climb two flights of warehouse stairs carrying inventory sheets without shortness of breath. Medications include amlodipine, vitamin D, and an over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg tablet he has taken twice daily for the past week to soothe an acromioclavicular strain after moving heavy shelving. He specifically denies aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants, glucocorticoids, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Family history notes a father who died of myocardial infarction at 78 and a mother with osteoarthritis; no relatives have bleeding disorders or chronic liver ailments. He quit smoking 18 years ago after a 20-pack-year exposure and drinks only non-alcoholic beer at sporting events. On arrival—before any intravenous access, fluids, vasoactive agents, antiemetics, acid suppressive therapy, or transfusion—he was seated upright on the stretcher, breathing comfortably, skin slightly pale but warm and dry, answering questions in complete sentences. Triaged vital signs obtained with the automatic cuff on the right arm level with the fourth intercostal space showed a blood pressure of 103/66 mm Hg and a tachycardic but regular pulse confirmed on three-lead telemetry at 126 beats per minute; respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute, oral temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Capillary refill was brisk at two seconds; sclerae were anicteric and conjunctivae only mildly blanched. There were no telangiectasias across the face, but faint spider angiomas were scattered over the upper chest and a subtle palmar erythema was noted, findings consistent with his known liver history. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated with the head of bed at 45°. Cardiac examination revealed a rapid but crisp S1 and S2 without gallop, rub, or murmur. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout. The abdomen was scaphoid and soft; gentle deep palpation elicited mild epigastric tenderness without guarding, rebound, masses, or detectable organomegaly. Shifting dullness was absent, and there was no flank bulging. Extremities showed no edema, cyanosis, or clubbing. Neurologic screen demonstrated intact orientation, fluent speech, symmetrical facial movements, 5/5 strength in all extremities, and normal finger-to-nose testing. A single 18-gauge catheter was inserted in the left antecubital vein strictly to obtain diagnostic blood samples; the patient had not yet received crystalloid or pharmacotherapy. Initial laboratory panel returned at 07:49: hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL, hematocrit 46 %, mean corpuscular volume 90 fL, platelet count 158 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.9 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 102 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 38 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 42 U/L, and international normalized ratio 1.18. An electrocardiogram printed concurrently displayed sinus tachycardia at 125 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Upright chest radiography showed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette, while a single supine abdominal film demonstrated a nonspecific gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. Digital rectal examination was deferred initially to avoid provoking further retching. The patient remained nil per os, under continuous cardiac monitoring, awaiting urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy to delineate the source of his acute upper gastrointestinal blood loss in the context of chronic hepatic parenchymal injury.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses eight pretreatment findings:
- BUN 10 mg/dL, below the first scoring threshold of 18.2 mg/dL: 0.
- Hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL in a man (≥13): 0.
- Systolic pressure 103 mm Hg (100–109): 1.
- Pulse 126/min (≥100): 1.
- Melena: 0. He reports brown stool; coffee-ground emesis is not melena.
- Syncope: explicitly denied, 0.
- Hepatic disease: persistent liver fibrosis with varices despite hepatitis C cure, 2.
- Heart failure: no history or clinical evidence, 0.
Total = 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 4.
Final answer: 4
